book: The Personality Brokers: The Strange History of Myers-Briggs and the Birth of Personality Testing
author: Merve Emre
en_title: The Personality Brokers: A Mother, a Daughter, and the Names of Personality
zh_deck: 从家庭观察到职业问卷，再到机构使用与商业出版。Merve Emre沿着一对母女的经历，追问十六型人格怎样来到我们面前。
en_deck: From domestic observation to questionnaires, institutional use, and publication: Emre restores the lives and decisions behind a familiar set of letters.

zh_title: 《MBTI的前世今生》：一对母女，怎样给性格起了名字
zh_body:
Merve Emre调查MBTI的历史时，找档案颇费周折。后来，她换了一个检索办法：不再只用创办者婚后的姓氏Briggs，而去查婚前的姓氏Cook。原先找不到的材料，终于在另一所大学出现了。

这段写作经历很适合用来认识本书。MBTI声称帮助人了解自己，发明者却早已被一个缩写遮住。许多人甚至不知道Myers和Briggs是两个女人的名字，更不知道她们是一对母女：Katharine Cook Briggs与Isabel Briggs Myers。

Emre本来做过管理咨询，在公司培训中接触过MBTI。成为文学研究者以后，她回头调查这个自己也使用过的工具。她没有写一本教人判断朋友属于哪种性格的指南，而是沿着母女的阅读、家庭生活、职业尝试与商业合作，追问一套分类怎样取得了今天这样的地位。

所以，读者要准备先放下手中的四个字母。这段历史不是从网络上的人格图表开始的，而是从一个母亲想知道孩子应当怎样长大开始的。

## 客厅里的实验室

Katharine把家庭生活当作研究对象，观察女儿，也收集其他母亲对孩子的记录。她后来认真研读荣格的《心理类型》，希望从中找到解释差异的办法。女儿Isabel则逐渐把这项兴趣带向职业世界，研究怎样使人和工作相配。

两代人的愿望既相通，又不完全一样。母亲关心教养，女儿更关心分工。Emre在访谈中解释，Isabel不满意某些测验把人区分为优劣或健全与不健全，希望各种类型都能找到合适的位置。二十世纪四十年代，她开始设计实际的问卷。这比母亲接触荣格要晚，不能把思想的开端与问卷的问世算成同一件事。

这层区别也改变了我们读母女故事的方式。她们不是坐下来商议怎样制造一件畅销产品，然后按计划走向成功。早年的观察、对家庭成员的困惑，以及对自己可以做什么的寻找，都慢慢进入了后来那份问卷。

书中还有一条容易令人意外的线索：Isabel写过推理小说，也把人格类型用于人物构思。分类与讲故事在这里有了联系。一个人物为什么这样选择，为什么与另一个人合不来，原本就是小说作者会追问的事。但解释得像一个故事，与经得起心理测量的检验，毕竟并不相同。

正是这种接近又不同的关系，使母女的业余身份值得认真讨论。她们确有长期观察人的经验，也有强烈的求知愿望；缺乏专业训练，却意味着方法仍需要检验。不能用“不过是两个家庭主妇”取消她们做过的工作，也不能因为她们曾被轻视，就替研究免除举证。

Emre的传记写法把这个矛盾保留下来。一个人可以富有抱负，同时深受时代观念限制；一种认识人的愿望，也可能在实行时变成安排人的办法。只要故事还跟着她们往下走，就很难把她们简化成天才发明家或江湖骗子。

## 问卷有了买主

问卷要离开家庭，得有人愿意使用。Isabel与人力管理顾问合作，把类型与岗位匹配的想法带进机构。早期买主还包括美国战略情报局的相关人员；在那里，问卷与其他心理评估、情境任务一起使用，并非单凭四个字母决定谁能当特工。

这一段历史颇能纠正今天的直觉。我们容易把人格测验当成个人兴趣：闲来测一测，找一个形容自己的名称。但组织很早就对它感兴趣，因为组织也面对识人和分工的难题。谁适合哪项任务，谁与谁可以合作，都需要作判断。

到了白领工作扩展的环境里，这种需求更明显。流水线上可以数产量，管理别人、与客户交涉的工作，却不那么容易只靠件数衡量。个人的谈吐、情绪和处事方式，都可能成为组织关心的对象。性格不再只是下班以后的私人话题。

由此，Isabel那句“让每种类型各得其所”，便出现了两种不同读法。对个人，它可以意味着不必因为自己与别人不同就处处自责；对组织，它也可以意味着把员工安置到最有利于运作的位置。两者有时一致，有时却会分开。员工想尝试的工作，不一定是组织最愿意让他做的工作。

这不是后来某个坏人把纯洁的工具用坏了那么简单。帮助人找到工作与帮助机构分配人，本来就一起出现在它的历史中。Emre最值得追问的地方正在这里：究竟谁有权解释“适合”，而当事人觉得不合适的时候，他的经验有没有同样的分量？

今天MBTI官方的伦理规范明确反对用它筛选求职者，也反对只凭类型决定职业方向。介绍历史时应当把这条边界说清，不能把过去的用途当成如今获准的用法。但历史仍能提醒我们，为何这些限制有必要：一种描述只要参与分配机会，就已经不只是轻松的自我认识游戏。

## 描述越宽，为什么越觉得像自己

问卷流通以后，还要面对另一个问题：类型描述写得多具体，使用者才会接受？

Emre在Longreads访谈中谈到一段出版过程。出版商希望把Isabel的描述改得更宽泛，好让更多人觉得适合自己；Isabel对此有疑虑。这个细节比笼统指责商业化更有意思，因为它指出了吸引力怎样进入文字内部。

描述很具体，读者可能立即说不符合；描述宽一些，则容易从自己的生活中找到相应片段。越多人能够认领，产品越容易传播。但这并不能反过来证明，它把人的差异分得更准确了。有时，恰恰因为说得不够明确，反例才不容易出现。

与此同时，这种认领也可能带来真实的宽慰。一个人第一次发现，原来自己并不是唯一需要独处的人，感受并不会因为量表有争议就自动变成假的。我们需要分辨的是，这份宽慰能证明什么，不能证明什么。

有关测量的问题，可以借一项书外研究说得更清楚。McCrae与Costa在1989年的研究中，没有找到支持那些截然二分的类型的证据，却发现部分量表维度与人格特质有关。这比“毫无内容”或“十六型都已被证实”更准确：问卷可能碰到了某些差异，分组的方法却不一定如名称显示得那么整齐。

这也解释了为什么本书没有变成一场彻底的辟谣。科学检验能讨论分类是否站得住，却不足以单独解释人们为何喜欢它。一个工具如何传播，既涉及测量，也涉及措辞、组织用途，以及人对自我说明的需要。Emre将这些线索放在一起，读者才有机会理解，为什么争议和流行能够长期并存。

不过，若最想读的是各种人格量表的技术比较，这本书并不够用。它的大量篇幅留给母女传记与文化史，论述科学问题时也带着批判立场。清楚这一点，才能决定自己想从书中得到什么，而不把一本历史叙事当成测量学教材。

## 连发明者也不止一种解释

Emre曾说，随着阅读母女的信件和生活材料，自己最初尖锐的态度有了变化。她仍然质疑这套分类，却越来越能理解，两位女性怎样试图把家庭中的知识变成受到承认的工作。

这个变化，也是本书形式上的一项收获。假如作者只为证明MBTI有问题，发明者的处境大可一笔带过；但传记不断给出新材料，迫使批评容纳此前没有看见的东西。对母女有了同情，并不妨碍检查她们的方法，反而让批评更难偷懒。

读者也可以把同样的耐心留给使用测验的人。有的人把它当游戏，有的人借它谈关系，有的人认真据此选择职业。这些用法的后果不同，不能只因使用了同一组字母，就把人归为一类。讽刺的是，批评分类时，我们也很容易再作一次过于简单的分类。

如今网络上还有大量借用四字母写法的测验，不都等于正式MBTI。16Personalities就说明自己采用另一套模型。因此，讨论一份结果之前，先确认它来自什么工具，比急着判断某个字母意味着什么更有用。

《MBTI的前世今生》最后留给人的，不只是对测验的怀疑。它让那些仿佛天然存在的名称重新有了历史：是谁写出来，怎样修改，经过哪些机构，才来到我们面前。知道这些，再说“我就是这种人”时，或许会稍微停一下。

四个字母可以是一个方便的话头，但母女漫长而并不整齐的一生已经说明，人的故事不会按分类表自行排好。要了解她们，还得去读信，查档案，看到那些不合预期的经历。要了解自己和身边的人，大概也省不掉这一部分。
en_body:
Researching the history of the MBTI, Merve Emre struggled to locate archival material. Eventually she changed her search: instead of looking only under the founder’s married name, Briggs, she tried her maiden name, Cook. Material that had been elusive turned up at another university.

This research experience offers a useful entrance to The Personality Brokers. A tool promising self-knowledge had obscured its inventors behind an acronym. Many users do not even know that Myers and Briggs were two women, let alone a mother and daughter: Katharine Cook Briggs and Isabel Briggs Myers.

Emre had encountered the MBTI during training when she worked in management consulting. After becoming a literary scholar, she returned to investigate it. The result is not a manual for identifying friends’ types. Following the women’s reading, domestic lives, vocational experiments, and business relationships, she asks how a classification acquired its present standing.

Readers should therefore be ready to set aside their own four letters for a while. This history begins not with online personality charts but with a mother trying to understand how a child should grow.

## A laboratory in the living room

Katharine treated family life as a subject of inquiry, observing her daughter and collecting other mothers’ records of their children. She later studied Jung’s Psychological Types closely, seeking an explanation of differences. Isabel gradually directed this interest toward working life and the question of matching people with jobs.

Their ambitions overlapped without being identical. The mother was concerned with education; the daughter increasingly with the division of work. As Emre explained in interview, Isabel disliked tests that divided people into better and worse, or healthy and unhealthy. She wanted each type to have an appropriate place. She began designing the actual questionnaire in the 1940s, later than her mother’s engagement with Jung. An intellectual starting point and the development of a questionnaire are not the same event.

This distinction changes the family story. The women did not sit down to plan a bestselling product and proceed directly toward success. Earlier observations, puzzles about family members, and their searches for something they themselves could do entered gradually into the eventual instrument.

Another unexpected strand is Isabel’s writing of detective fiction and her use of personality types in constructing characters. Classification meets storytelling here. Why does someone choose this action? Why can two people not get along? These are a novelist’s questions too. But an explanation that makes a convincing story is not necessarily a claim that survives psychometric testing.

This proximity and difference make the women’s amateur status worth considering carefully. They had experience observing people and a powerful desire to learn. A lack of professional training nevertheless left methods requiring scrutiny. Dismissing their work because they were housewives is no better than exempting it from evidence because they had been overlooked.

Biography preserves the tension. An ambitious person can also be limited by her time’s assumptions. A desire to understand people can become a way to arrange them. Following these women through their lives makes it difficult to reduce them either to inspired geniuses or to frauds.

## The questionnaire finds buyers

For the questionnaire to leave the home, others had to be willing to use it. Isabel worked with a personnel consultant and took the idea of matching types to jobs into organizations. Early purchasers included people connected with the Office of Strategic Services. There, the questionnaire formed part of assessment alongside other psychological measures and situational tasks. Four letters alone did not determine who could be a secret agent.

This history challenges a contemporary assumption. Personality tests can appear to be private entertainment: take one in spare time and find a description of yourself. Organizations had an early interest because they also faced problems of identification and assignment. They wanted to judge who suited a task and who could work with whom.

The expansion of white-collar employment sharpened those concerns. Production on an assembly line could be counted in units. Managing people or dealing with clients was less easily measured that way. Speech, temperament, and habits of interaction became organizational interests. Personality was no longer something belonging only to life after work.

The hope that each type might find its place consequently acquired two readings. For individuals it could mean relief from blaming themselves for being different. For an organization it could mean placing employees where they best served operations. The purposes can coincide, but they can also diverge. An employee may want to try something other than the role an employer thinks most suitable.

This is more complex than a bad actor corrupting an originally innocent tool. Helping people find work and helping institutions allocate people were intertwined in its history. The question becomes who gets to define suitability, and whether the individual’s contrary experience counts equally.

Current MBTI ethical guidance explicitly opposes using type to screen job applicants or making career decisions from type alone. Historical practices must not be presented as currently authorized uses. Yet the history also clarifies why such boundaries matter. Once a description helps allocate opportunities, it is more than a lighthearted exercise in self-recognition.

## Why can a broader description feel more accurate?

As the questionnaire circulated, another question arose: how specific should a description be if users were to accept it?

In her Longreads interview, Emre discussed a publishing episode in which the publisher wanted Isabel’s descriptions broadened so that more people could recognize themselves. Isabel had reservations. This is more informative than a general accusation of commercialization. It identifies how appeal enters the wording itself.

A specific description allows a reader to say it does not fit. A broader one makes it easier to retrieve some matching experience. More people can claim it, and the product travels further. That popularity does not establish more accurate distinctions. Sometimes imprecision simply makes counterexamples harder to find.

Recognition can nevertheless provide genuine comfort. Someone may be relieved to discover that they are not alone in needing solitude. Disagreement about a scale’s validity does not make the relief imaginary. What must be separated is what that feeling can demonstrate and what it cannot.

A study outside the book helps clarify the measurement issue. In 1989, McCrae and Costa found no support for sharply dichotomous types, while finding relationships between some scales and personality traits. This is more precise than either saying the questionnaire measures nothing or declaring all sixteen types proven. It may register differences without sorting them as neatly as the labels suggest.

This also helps explain why the book is not merely a debunking exercise. Scientific examination can question whether categories hold up, but cannot alone explain their attraction. A tool spreads through language, organizational uses, and the need for self-description as well as measurement. Bringing these threads together makes the coexistence of controversy and popularity intelligible.

Readers primarily seeking a technical comparison of personality measures will still need other books. Much of this one concerns the women’s biographies and cultural history, and its treatment of scientific questions has a critical orientation. It is worth knowing what kind of inquiry one is opening, rather than treating historical narrative as a psychometrics textbook.

## Even the inventors require more than one explanation

Emre has described her attitude changing as she read the women’s correspondence and personal records. She continued to question the classification, while understanding more fully their efforts to make domestic knowledge into recognized work.

That change is one achievement of the biographical form. If the only purpose were to demonstrate the MBTI’s defects, the inventors’ circumstances could be passed over. Instead, new material requires criticism to accommodate what it had not seen. Sympathy does not replace examination of method; it makes criticism less able to take shortcuts.

Readers can extend similar patience to test users. Some treat it as a game, others as a language for relationships, still others as a serious basis for career choices. Their uses have different consequences. Sharing a letter code does not make the users interchangeable. Criticizing classification can itself become an occasion for careless classification.

Many contemporary online tests also borrow four-letter formats without being the official MBTI. The 16Personalities site, for instance, explains that it uses a different model. Before interpreting a result, identifying the instrument is more useful than assuming its letters settle what it means.

The book leaves us with more than skepticism. Names that seemed natural acquire a history: who wrote them, how they were revised, which institutions carried them to us. Knowing that history may introduce a pause before “This is simply who I am.”

Four letters can open a conversation. The women’s long and untidy lives show why they cannot complete it. Understanding them requires letters, archives, and experiences that resist expectation. Understanding ourselves and those around us is unlikely to dispense with the equivalent work.

Luo Xiangjie’s Traditional Chinese translation was retitled MBTI的前世今生 by Walkers in 2026 without new content; earlier titles include 「性格」贩子 and 你是哪一型人？. This is a 2018 book, not a new personality diagnosis guide.
